einzeiler: The origins of the gay rights movement from the 1950s up to the Stonewall Uprising.
kurzfassung: This episode explores the roots of the American gay rights movement in the 1950s, detailing the formation of early clandestine groups like the Mattachine Society and the Daughters of Bilitis. It highlights the severe legal, medical, and governmental discrimination faced by gay individuals, including aggressive conversion therapies and FBI surveillance. Despite these obstacles, activists fought back through landmark court victories and pioneering publications that laid the groundwork for future liberation.
stichpunkte: The Stonewall Uprising of 1969 served as a pivotal turning point that brought LGBTQ activism out of the shadows.
In 1950s America, severe state laws and sodomy statutes made living openly as a gay person a de facto crime.
Harry Hay and a close circle of friends founded the secretive Mattachine Society in Los Angeles to advocate for gay rights.
Dale Jennings secured a landmark court acquittal in 1952 after exposing police entrapment.
The Daughters of Bilitis formed in 1955 as the first national lesbian organization, creating their own publication called The Ladder.
Psychological establishments classified homosexuality as a mental disorder in 1952, leading to widespread conversion therapies.
Evelyn Hooker published a groundbreaking 1956 study proving that gay men were just as psychologically well-adjusted as straight men.
The FBI and J. Edgar Hoover maintained extensive surveillance on gay organizations and government workers.
One Magazine successfully defeated U.S. Post Office obscenity charges at the Supreme Court, expanding free speech protections.

beschreibung:
In the summer of 1969, a police raid on the Stonewall Inn sparked a riot on the streets of Greenwich Village. The protest marked a turning point in the gay rights movement. But the famed resistance in New York capped a movement that had been building for nearly two decades in America, as LGBTQ people mobilized to fight widespread and pervasive discrimination.
In the years following World War II, members of the LGBTQ community faced broad discrimination — from strict laws that oppressed them, churches that declared their very existence sinful, and a government that demonized them. They would push back against the American Psychological Association, the FBI and finally, the courts. Slowly, LGBTQ activism would emerge from out of the closet and onto the American scene.
This series follows strands of the gay rights movement in America from 1950 until 1970. But it’s just the beginning of a story about a fight for social and political equality — a battle that’s still being fought today.
